---
title: "Open problems"
subtitle: "Eighteen research questions spanning colony dynamics, control, climate, landscape, and data"
---

[Research agenda]{.eyebrow}

The working review consolidates sixteen domain problems and two cross-cutting methodological questions. The numbering below follows that manuscript. These are research directions rather than settled claims; each problem should be tied to measurable outcomes, identifiable parameters, and a decision or experiment that would change as a result.

## Persistence, tipping points, and collapse

### P1 — Basin boundary characterisation

Characterise the boundary between viable-colony and extinction basins in reduced colony models. This geometry is the foundation for a composite stress score and state-dependent management.

### P2 — Mechanism identification

Determine when monitoring data can distinguish alternative collapse pathways, such as demographic feedback, parasitism, thermal stress, or combinations of these mechanisms.

## Parasites and pathogens

### P3 — Multi-virus coinfection

Develop and analyse models in which several viruses interact within a colony rather than treating a single virus in isolation.

### P4 — Cross-taxon parasite interaction

Model interactions between *Varroa destructor*, *Nosema*, viruses, and their host colony, using surveillance data to determine which couplings materially change persistence or collapse risk.

### P5 — Treatment-induced destabilisation

Determine whether and when a treatment perturbation can move a stressed colony across a basin boundary even while reducing its target parasite or pathogen.

## Climate, thermoregulation, and agrochemicals

### P6 — Stochastic collapse-time distribution

Use stochastic differential equations and first-passage theory to quantify how environmental variability changes the probability and timing of colony collapse.

### P7 — Pesticide catastrophe criterion

Derive a dynamical threshold for pesticide-driven loss of the viable-colony attractor, including cumulative and sublethal exposure where data permit.

### P8 — Critical phenological offset

Quantify how much mismatch between floral-resource availability and colony nutritional demand can be tolerated before persistence is lost.

### P9 — Thermal exposure functionals

Identify temperature summaries that retain the duration, severity, and timing of heat or cold stress better than seasonal mean temperature alone.

## Management and control

### P10 — Multi-stressor optimal control

Formulate joint intervention policies for mites, nutrition, pathogens, and seasonal stress rather than optimising one intervention independently.

### P11 — Viable-split separatrix

Characterise the initial combinations of bees, brood, resources, queen state, and timing that separate successful colony splits from failed splits.

### P12 — Near-optimal feedback rules

Derive simple, field-usable decision rules and bound their loss relative to a fully optimised control policy.

### P13 — Economic portfolio optimisation

Optimise how a commercial operation allocates limited labour, treatments, feeding, replacement queens, and monitoring effort across many colonies.

## Spatial, landscape, and multispecies dynamics

### P14 — Coupled ODE–PDE well-posedness

Establish a rigorous framework for coupling within-colony ODE dynamics to spatial resource, exposure, or foraging PDEs.

### P15 — Apiary network stability

Determine when drift, robbing, migration, or management links allow one declining colony to destabilise neighbouring colonies or an apiary network.

### P16 — Managed–wild competition and mutualism collapse

Analyse how managed and wild pollinators compete for resources and how those dynamics feed back on plant–pollinator mutualisms.

## Cross-cutting methodology

### Early-warning lead-time bounds

Derive the maximum useful warning time near saddle-node and subcritical Hopf bifurcations as a function of noise and parameter drift. Test whether combining acoustic, thermal, and manual observations can provably improve lead time.

### Hybrid-model identifiability

Establish which latent states and parameters in mechanistic–machine-learning models can be estimated from realistic monitoring streams, and determine the minimum observation frequency and diversity needed.

::: {.panel-dark}
### Priority entry points

The working review identifies basin-boundary characterisation, cross-taxon parasite interaction, critical phenological offset, and the viable-split separatrix as high-value entry points: each is tractable with current methods, has a plausible validation pathway, and unlocks related questions.
:::
